predictions.title: Cached-rollout agent fine-tuning reaches a second open framework by H1 2027
predictions.body: The June 12 arXiv paper CacheRL (arXiv:2606.14179) attacks the most expensive part of teaching a small model to use tools well: reinforcement learning over multi-turn tool use normally has to run the real tools live thousands of times per training batch, which dominates cost and makes the loop slow and brittle. CacheRL removes the live tool calls by replaying a three-tier fuzzy cache of past trajectories with token-level masking, and pairs that with a cache-tier-aware hybrid reward that reweights answer quality so the model is not punished for gaps the cache itself introduced. The reported numbers are the kind that get a method copied rather than admired: 92% process accuracy on multi-step tool-calling, within striking distance of GPT-5's reported 94%, while using roughly 100x less compute, and lifting validation reward on Qwen3-4B-Thinking from 0.43 to 0.78, with ablations crediting a 17% gain to the cache-aware reward. The structural reason this spreads is that the bottleneck it removes is universal: every team doing agent RL on open models — and the major open post-training libraries (TRL, verl, OpenRLHF, SkyRL, ART, NeMo-RL) plus inference-coupled rollout stacks — pays the same live-tool-execution tax, and a cached-replay rollout with a tier-aware reward is a drop-in substitution for the rollout phase rather than a new model architecture, which is exactly the shape of technique that diffuses fast. The forward thesis is that cached-rollout (replay-instead-of-live-execution) RL for tool-calling agents hardens from a single paper into a supported training mode that practitioners can pick up off the shelf. The concrete, falsifiable landing: by H1 2027 (on or before 2027-06-30) EITHER a mainstream open agent-RL or post-training framework other than the CacheRL authors' own code — TRL, verl, OpenRLHF, SkyRL, ART, NeMo-RL, or a comparably adopted open library — ships documented, first-class support for a cached or replayed rollout mode (offline trajectory replay with masking in place of live tool execution) for multi-turn tool-calling RL, OR at least one independent group publishes a reproduction that releases open weights or training code applying cached-rollout RL to a different base model family and reports tool-calling accuracy within ten points of a frontier model at an order-of-magnitude-lower rollout cost. What does NOT count: a closed or hosted-only service that merely offers 'cheaper agent RL' without a documented cached-replay rollout path; a generic prompt or trajectory cache used only for inference rather than for the RL rollout loop; a citation, benchmark mention, or blog reference to CacheRL with no shipped feature or released artifact; or a follow-up from the original authors on the same codebase. If by June 30, 2027 cached-rollout RL remains confined to the original CacheRL paper and its own repository, with no second framework feature and no independent open reproduction on a different model, the prediction fails.

reasoning.because: CacheRL (June 12) hit 92% tool-calling accuracy near GPT-5 at ~100x less compute via cached rollouts
reasoning.given: every open agent-RL stack pays the same live-execution tax; cached replay is a drop-in rollout swap
reasoning.so_that: a second open RL framework ships a cached-rollout mode, or an independent group reproduces it on another model
reasoning.landing: by H1 2027 (2027-06): 2nd framework feature or independent open reproduction
reasoning.plain_language: A new trick trains tool-using AI 100x cheaper by replaying old runs instead of re-running real tools; soon other training kits copy it.

predictions.summary: CacheRL trains tool-calling agents with replayed cached rollouts instead of costly live tool calls, reporting 92% accuracy near GPT-5 at ~100x less compute. Since every open agent-RL stack pays that live-execution tax, expect cached-rollout training to land in a second open framework by H1 2027.

predictions.title: Omnigent ships as a paid Databricks-managed agent-orchestration tier by Q2 2027
predictions.body: Databricks introduced Omnigent on June 13 as an Apache 2.0, alpha-stage meta-harness: a layer that sits above individual coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Pi) and agent SDKs (OpenAI Agents, Claude Agents SDK) so a developer drives several of them through one interface, with stateful policies, cost budgets, permissions and OS-level sandboxing enforced at the meta-harness layer, plus shareable live sessions and cloud execution on Modal and Daytona sandboxes. Crucially it was published as a standalone OSS project on GitHub (omnigent-ai/omnigent) rather than a Databricks-only feature, and it landed alongside the Data + AI Summit. The business read is that this is the opening move of an open-core go-to-market, not a charity release: the same playbook that built Databricks around open-source Spark and Delta. Giving away the orchestration and policy layer seeds adoption and makes Omnigent the default control point a team standardizes on; the durable revenue is the managed runtime, hosted execution, identity and governance, and enterprise support that sit underneath it. The forward thesis is that Databricks converts that adoption into a commercial, first-party managed offering on its own platform. The concrete, falsifiable landing: by Q2 2027 Databricks publicly offers a priced, Databricks-hosted Omnigent-based agent-orchestration product - a managed runtime, hosted/cloud execution, or enterprise governance tier that is generally available or in a paid preview - announced by Databricks (blog, pricing page, Data + AI Summit / keynote, or a Databricks press release) and tied to Databricks-billed consumption (DBUs) or a subscription. What does NOT count: the OSS repo staying free with no paid Databricks-hosted tier; a third party (not Databricks) commercializing it; a free managed preview with no path to billing; an unpriced 'coming soon' teaser; or a generic Databricks agent product that does not build on or productize Omnigent. The counter-risk is that Databricks keeps Omnigent purely community OSS and monetizes agents only through its existing Mosaic AI / Agent Bricks surface, leaving Omnigent itself unmonetized through mid-2027.

reasoning.because: Databricks open-sourced the Omnigent meta-harness (Apache 2.0) June 13 as a standalone OSS project
reasoning.given: Open-core is the proven data-platform GTM: free the layer, charge for managed runtime + governance
reasoning.so_that: Databricks ships a paid managed Omnigent tier with hosted execution, cost/permission governance and an SLA
reasoning.landing: by Q2 2027; a priced Databricks-hosted Omnigent product, GA or paid preview
reasoning.plain_language: Databricks gave away the free tool that runs many AI agents, so it will likely sell a paid hosted version companies pay for.

predictions.summary: Databricks open-sourced Omnigent, a meta-harness over multiple coding agents, as a standalone Apache 2.0 project alongside its Data + AI Summit. That mirrors the open-core playbook behind Spark and Delta, so by Q2 2027 Databricks should offer a priced, hosted Omnigent orchestration tier.

predictions.title: Agent meta-harness becomes the cross-vendor policy plane for agents by H1 2027
predictions.body: Databricks open-sourcing Omnigent on June 13 introduces a meta-harness that sits one layer above individual coding agents and agent SDKs, wrapping Claude Code, Codex, Pi, OpenAI Agents and the Claude Agents SDK behind one interface so implementations can be swapped without rewriting. The structurally significant part is not the unified driver surface but where the guardrails live: Omnigent enforces stateful, contextual policy at the meta-harness layer itself, tracking each wrapped agent's actions and applying cost budgets, permissions and OS-level sandboxing across whichever runtime is underneath. That relocates the natural control point for enterprise agent governance upward, from per-runtime configuration scattered across each vendor's own harness to a single vendor-neutral layer that brokers, observes and constrains them all. The prediction is that this stops being one Databricks OSS project and becomes a recognized architectural tier. By H1 2027, expect at least one more independent vendor or hyperscaler to ship an agent meta-harness whose headline capability is enforcing policy (budgets, permissions, sandboxing, or audit) uniformly across two or more rival agent runtimes, or an enterprise-agent governance framework to name the meta-harness layer as the prescribed policy-enforcement point. What does NOT count: a single-vendor harness that only governs its own agents, an orchestration or routing tool with no cross-runtime guardrail enforcement, a marketing claim of multi-agent support without policy applied at the wrapping layer, or Omnigent itself merely adding more wrapped agents.

reasoning.because: Databricks open-sourced Omnigent, a meta-harness wrapping Claude Code, Codex and agent SDKs as one
reasoning.given: Whoever owns the layer above rival agent runtimes owns where cross-vendor agent policy is enforced
reasoning.so_that: Enterprise agent governance shifts up from per-runtime config to a vendor-neutral meta-harness policy plane
reasoning.landing: by H1 2027; a 2nd vendor or hyperscaler ships cross-runtime agent policy
reasoning.plain_language: A new tool sits above rival AI coding agents and lets companies set one set of safety and cost rules for all of them.

predictions.summary: Databricks open-sourced Omnigent, a meta-harness wrapping Claude Code, Codex and agent SDKs behind one interface while enforcing cost budgets, permissions and sandboxing at that layer. By H1 2027, expect a second vendor to ship a meta-harness enforcing policy across rival agent runtimes.
